blocks.text: Imagine a library where frequently accessed books are kept on a small shelf near the entrance, while less popular books are stored in a large warehouse. This is similar to how caches work in computer systems.

blocks.markdown: Caches are small, fast storage locations that hold copies of data from frequently accessed main memory locations. They bridge the speed gap between the fast CPU and slower main memory.

blocks.title: Cache Line
blocks.text: A cache line is the smallest unit of data that can be transferred between the cache and main memory. It typically consists of multiple contiguous bytes.

blocks.markdown: Caches can be organized in different ways. Two common types are direct-mapped and set-associative caches. Let's explore these configurations.

blocks.title: Direct-Mapped Cache
blocks.text: In a direct-mapped cache, each block of main memory maps to exactly one cache line. The cache index is determined by the address modulo the number of cache lines.

blocks.title: Set-Associative Cache
blocks.text: A set-associative cache divides the cache into several sets, each containing multiple lines. A memory block maps to any line within a specific set, allowing more flexibility than direct-mapped caches.

blocks.title: Calculating Cache Hit Rate
blocks.prompt: Given a sequence of memory accesses and a cache configuration, calculate the cache hit rate.

steps.text: Consider a direct-mapped cache with 4 lines and a sequence of memory accesses: 0, 4, 8, 0, 4, 8, 12.
Determine the cache line for each access using the formula: `index = address % number_of_lines`.
Track hits and misses. A hit occurs if the data is already in the cache line; otherwise, it's a miss.
Calculate the hit rate as the number of hits divided by the total number of accesses.

blocks.answer: The hit rate is 4/7 or approximately 57%.

blocks.title: Effect of Cache Line Size on Spatial Locality
blocks.prompt: Explain how increasing the cache line size affects spatial locality.

steps.text: Spatial locality refers to the tendency of a program to access data locations that are close to each other.
Larger cache lines can hold more contiguous data, potentially capturing more spatial locality.
However, larger lines may also increase the chance of loading unnecessary data, known as cache pollution.

blocks.answer: Increasing cache line size can improve spatial locality by capturing more contiguous data, but may also lead to cache pollution.

blocks.title: Key Point
blocks.text: Cache performance is influenced by the cache organization, line size, and the access pattern of the program.

points: Caches are small, fast storage that improve access times for frequently used data.
Direct-mapped caches are simple but can suffer from conflict misses.
Set-associative caches offer flexibility but are more complex.
Cache line size affects spatial locality and cache pollution.
